profile.campus: Arcola Business Park, Stone Ridge, Brambleton, Loudoun County, Virginia (Microsoft 'IAD11' data center)
profile.address: Growth Mindset Lane, Arcola Tech Park, Brambleton, Loudoun County, Virginia, 20107
profile.reading:
This building sits in the Arcola Business Park in Stone Ridge, Brambleton, Loudoun County, Virginia, matching the location Bisnow identified in county planning documents as Microsoft's "IAD11" data center: a $400 million, 500,000-square-foot building on 67 acres, sited between two Amazon-owned parcels also designated for data center development. Microsoft purchased the underlying property in August 2020 for $93.7 million and received expedited site plan approval that let construction proceed once permitting was complete without a rezoning process, working with Turner Construction as general contractor, Dewberry as engineer, and Gensler as architect. Bisnow reported the project faced minimal community opposition, unlike some other regional data center proposals, largely because the site's zoning had already been approved for the use. IAD11 is one of several Microsoft data centers across Northern Virginia, alongside facilities in Ashburn, Leesburg, Sterling, Manassas City, and Prince William County; Loudoun County's own economic development office has said data centers contributed $859 million in county tax revenue in 2025, with computer equipment personal property tax from data centers making up roughly $670.3 million of that, the county's single largest personal property tax source. Microsoft has not published IAD11's current operational status, opening date, or MW capacity, so this registry records the reported 500,000-square-foot, 67-acre, $400 million project description as the most specific available figures for this address.

Dominion Energy, the regional utility serving Loudoun and Prince William counties, has repeatedly cited Northern Virginia data center growth as the largest driver of new electricity demand in its Virginia service territory in filings with the Virginia State Corporation Commission, prompting new transmission and generation investment; Virginia's data center sales-and-use tax exemption, administered by the Virginia Economic Development Partnership, has been a material factor cited by state and local officials in why Microsoft and other hyperscalers have concentrated so much investment in this specific corridor rather than spreading it across lower-tax states.

reading.body:
Microsoft has not published IAD11's power capacity, so its scale relative to other facilities cannot be determined from operator specifications. The building itself measures 500,000 square feet on 67 acres and cost $400 million to develop, placing it among the larger single structures in the Northern Virginia corridor, though building size does not directly indicate electrical load. Microsoft purchased the site in 2020 and received expedited approval for construction as a data center, but the current operational status and opening date are not published.

Northern Virginia concentrates hyperscaler investment partly because Virginia's data center sales-and-use tax exemption reduces operating costs compared to other states. Loudoun County alone reported data centers generated $859 million in tax revenue in 2025, with computer equipment personal property tax from data centers accounting for roughly $670 million of that sum, making data centers the county's single largest source of personal property tax. Dominion Energy, the regional utility, has identified Northern Virginia data center growth as the largest driver of new electricity demand in its Virginia service territory.

IAD11 sits among 326 mapped data center facilities statewide, only 23 of which publish power capacity figures. Virginia's published capacity totals 1,375.4 megawatts across those 23 facilities. Without published specifications for this campus, it cannot be ranked by capacity and therefore cannot be assessed as a constraint on AI scaling in the state.
